summary: Analyzes the solutions proposed for hosts to learn whether IPv6 addresses are being synthesized and which NAT64 prefix and format are used. It concludes by recommending standardization of the approach based on heuristic discovery.

plainLanguage.summary: A NAT64 device lets IPv6-only hosts reach IPv4 servers by turning IPv4 addresses into IPv6 addresses. A host that does not know about the translator cannot tell a translated address from a real one. This RFC compares nine ways a host could find out, and recommends the simplest: a DNS query for a well-known name.

questions: how do hosts learn the nat64 prefix
subtitle: How a host can find out that its IPv6 address was translated, and which prefix the translator used.

tldr.problem: In an IPv6-only access network, a NAT64 translator plus a DNS64 server let IPv6 hosts reach IPv4 servers. A host that does not know this is happening cannot tell a translated address from a real one, and cannot build a translated address for an IPv4 literal it already knows.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyses nine ways a host could learn that synthesis is happening and which prefix is used, from guessing the prefix out of a DNS answer to new EDNS0 options, a new DNS record type, DHCPv6, router advertisements, STUN attributes and access-technology signalling. Each is scored against five issues the solutions have to handle.
tldr.outcome: The authors recommend publishing the heuristic method based on a DNS query for a well-known name as a Standards Track document. Their general principle is to keep the solution minimal, avoid touching entities that are not otherwise involved, and require little or no network-side operation.

today: RFC 7051 is an Informational RFC published in November 2013. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the survey of ways to learn a NAT64 prefix, and its recommendation is to publish the heuristic discovery method as a Standards Track document.

sections.title: The Five Issues
sections.content:
Hosts and applications may benefit from learning whether an IPv6 address is synthesized, which would mean that a NAT64 is used to reach the IPv4 network or Internet. Two issues can be addressed with solutions that let hosts and applications learn the Network-Specific Prefix used by the NAT64 and DNS64 devices.

The first issue, Issue #1, is finding out whether a particular address is synthetic, and therefore learning the presence of a NAT64. A dual-stack host with IPv4 connectivity could use that information to bypass NAT64 and use native IPv4 transport for destinations that are reachable through IPv4. The second issue, Issue #2, is finding out how to construct from an IPv4 address an IPv6 address that will be routable to and by the NAT64. That is useful when IPv4 literals turn up in the payload of a protocol, or when an application does not use DNS and knows the IPv4 address by some other means.

Three further issues have to be considered by any solution. Issue #3 asks whether DNS is required at all, since a host that does not implement DNS cannot use it to learn the prefix. Issue #4 is about supporting a changing prefix: the prefix a host learned can go stale when the host moves to a network with a different prefix, or when the network operator changes it. Issue #5 is about supporting several prefixes, which a network may use for load balancing, with each NAT64 device in the same network having its own prefix. Learning a single prefix is enough for a host to synthesise an address locally, but to avoid NAT64 the host needs to learn all of them.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC sorts the problem into five questions: is this address translated, which prefix was used, can it be answered without DNS, what happens when the prefix changes, and what if there is more than one prefix.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
Address synthesis is the mechanism where an IPv4 address is represented as an IPv6 address that the NAT64 understands. The synthesised IPv6 address is formed by embedding the IPv4 address as it is into an IPv6 address prefixed with the NSP or the WKP, with the unused suffix bits set to zero as described in Section 2.2 of RFC 6052.

DNS64 is a network entity that synthesises IPv6 addresses and AAAA records out of IPv4 addresses and A records, which makes IPv4 namespaces visible in the IPv6 namespace. It uses the NSP and or the WKP in the synthesis process. NAT64 is the network entity that translates IPv6 packets to IPv4 packets and back; IPv6 packets sent to addresses in the NSP or WKP are routed to it, and it is the entity a host or application may want to avoid or to use.

The Network-Specific Prefix is a prefix chosen by a network administrator for NAT64 and DNS64 to present IPv4 addresses in the IPv6 namespace. The Well-Known Prefix is a prefix, 64:ff9b::/96, chosen by the IETF and configured by a network administrator for the same purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: The NSP is a prefix the network operator picks, and the WKP is one the IETF picked for everyone. NAT64 and DNS64 use one of them to wrap IPv4 addresses inside IPv6 addresses.

sections.title: Why a Host Would Want to Know
sections.content:
Certain applications operating in protocol translation scenarios benefit from knowing the IPv6 prefix used by a local NAT64. This applies to Scenario 1, an IPv6 network to the IPv4 Internet, Scenario 5, an IPv6 network to an IPv4 network, and Scenario 7, the IPv6 Internet to the IPv4 Internet, in the IPv4/IPv6 translation framework. Scenario 3 is not considered applicable, because there the NAT64 sits at the front of a remote IPv4 network and a host in the IPv6 Internet gains very little from learning its prefix.

The RFC lists the use cases. For host-based DNSSEC validation, synthetic AAAA records cannot be validated in a host, so a security-aware host has to perform the DNS64 function locally, and to do that it must learn the WKP or the proper NSP. For protocols that use IPv4 literals, an IPv6-only access network cannot create native IPv4 connections, but with a NAT64 present the host can synthesise an IPv6 address by combining the IPv4 literal with the prefix NAT64 uses. Multicast translation is a third case. URI schemes with host IPv4 address literals are a fourth, where a host can synthesise an IPv6 address out of the literal and connect over IPv6. Finally, a host can update its address preference table to prefer native prefixes over translated ones, which helps because applications are more likely to traverse NAT44 than NAT64.

The difficulty is that DNS64 cannot serve applications that do not use DNS or that receive a referral as an IPv4 literal address. The Session Description Protocol, as used by RTSP and SIP, is one example, and web browsers are another, because IPv4 literals still turn up in web pages and URLs.
sections.plainLanguage: Knowing the prefix lets a host check signatures on DNS answers itself, connect to an IPv4 server it only knows the IPv4 address of, and prefer native addresses over translated ones. The trouble is that some applications never ask DNS at all.

sections.title: The Nine Candidate Solutions
sections.content:
The RFC analyses nine proposals, each described in the same shape: what it is, what it solves, and what it costs.

The first asks DNS for the AAAA record of a well-known IPv4-only name. A negative answer means no DNS64 and no NAT64 are present; a positive one means synthesis is happening, and the host can guess the prefix by subtracting the known IPv4 address from the returned IPv6 address. It needs no host stack or resolver change and no support from the network, but it does need someone to host the record, and it finds only one prefix unless several synthetic records are returned.

The second and third use EDNS0. One adds an option with three flag bits, the SY-bits, where values other than 000 and 111 give the prefix length explicitly; the other puts three flag bits in the EDNS0 OPT header itself. Both need changes to hosts and to DNS64 servers, and both are limited because EDNS0 options and flags are typically hop-by-hop only, so they survive only if the EDNS0-capable DNS64 is the first DNS server the host talks to. The RFC notes that the flag-bit variant consumes scarce bits from the OPT header and is unlikely to be accepted.

The fourth proposes a dedicated A64 DNS resource record holding one IPv4-embedded IPv6 address. It tells a host plainly that the address is not native, but it does not help with Issue #2 or Issue #3, it needs a new record type in both resolvers and servers, and it adds load: a dual-stack host may issue three queries, for A64, AAAA and A.

The fifth uses DNS in two other ways: a TXT record with a well-known string followed by the NAT64 address and prefix length, and a URI-enabled NAPTR query whose input name is the same one a reverse lookup would use, in the .ip6.arpa. tree. The U-NAPTR variant needs provisioning in that tree, which is no longer entirely internal to the provider, and the iterative search can take several queries. The RFC also notes that RFC 5507 recommends against reusing TXT records to expand DNS.

The sixth and seventh move the information into IP configuration. A DHCPv6 option can carry the unicast, any-source multicast and source-specific multicast prefixes with their lengths, and another proposal would use a DHCPv6 option to communicate the prefix used for building IPv4-converted IPv6 addresses together with the format type and the synthesis algorithm. A Router Advertisement option, called OPTION_AFT_PREFIX_RA, carries the same prefixes as the DHCPv6 option. Both hook into the configuration phase and avoid DNS, but both need a new option and changes to hosts, and both need network nodes that are not otherwise part of the NAT64 and DNS64 deployment to be configured and managed. The RFC judges the DHCPv6 approach the better of the two, because management can be centralised in a few DHCPv6 servers rather than repeated in every access router.

The eighth uses STUN, or a similar application-layer protocol. The host sends a STUN request with a new SENDING-TO attribute holding the IPv6 address it sent to, and the server replies with a new RECEIVED-AS attribute holding the address the request arrived on; comparing the two reveals a candidate prefix. The true IPv4 destination address is used, which may be more reliable than the one DNS returned, and the client learns its public IPv4 address in the same exchange. But a server has to answer the queries, the protocol needs standardising on both sides, and the RFC calls it heavyweight for an application that does not otherwise use STUN. The ninth proposal uses the attachment-time signalling of the access technology itself, such as the 3GPP Non-Access-Stratum protocol, to list all the prefixes during network access establishment. It solves the most issues of the nine, but it needs a new parameter for every access system of interest, and changes to the link layers are slow and laborious.
sections.plainLanguage: The nine options fall into three groups: guessing the prefix from DNS, carrying it explicitly in DNS or in IP configuration, and asking a server on the network. Every one of them has to change something somewhere.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.content:
The conclusion is to recommend publishing the well-known DNS name heuristic discovery method as a Standards Track IETF document, for applications and host implementors to implement as it stands. The general principle behind that is to have a solution as minimal as possible, to avoid impacts on entities that are not otherwise involved in the protocol translation scheme, to minimise the impact on hosts, and to require minimal to no operational effort on the network side.

Of the five issues, the authors give the most weight to Issues #1 and #2. They give little weight to Issue #3, because cases where hosts need to synthesise IPv6 addresses but have no DNS available seem rare, and an application that does not otherwise use DNS ought to be able to trigger a simple DNS query to find the WKP or NSP. Issue #4 is handled by most of the solutions, and Issue #5 is considered mostly insignificant, since even if individual hosts use only one prefix at a time, different hosts would be using different prefixes, which already supports load balancing targets.

The reasoning behind the recommendation is that the DNS64 entity has to be configured with the WKP or NSP in order to synthesise at all, so using DNS to deliver the synthesis information is logical. The synthesis information shares the fate of the DNS response, which reduces the chance of stale prefix information being handed out. Having every DNS64 server support explicit discovery is hard to arrange, though: the U-NAPTR approach needs provisioning in the .ip6.arpa. tree, which is not entirely internal to the provider, DHCPv6 needs extra configuration and hosts must have DHCPv6 clients, and router advertisement mechanisms are operationally expensive because the configuration has to be placed and maintained in the access routers. Both DHCPv6 and router advertisements also involve entities that would not otherwise need to know about protocol translation. Finally, a host does not have to implement STUN, whereas DNS is required in practice anyway, and STUN would need changing on both the host and the network side.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors recommend the simplest option: a host asks DNS for a well-known name and works the prefix out from the answer. It needs nothing new from the network, and the prefix ages with the DNS record.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations are essentially the same as those described in DNS64 (RFC 6147). The document also covers the man-in-the-middle and denial-of-service attacks that come from forging the information needed to synthesise IPv6 addresses from IPv4 ones. Forgery may allow an attacker to insert itself as a man in the middle, or to mount a denial-of-service attack.

The DHCPv6 and router advertisement approaches are vulnerable to forgery, because an attacker may send forged router advertisements or act as a rogue DHCPv6 server, unless DHCPv6 authentication or Secure Neighbor Discovery is used. If an attacker can already modify and forge DNS responses, then the ability to influence local address synthesis is likely to be of little additional value. A DNS-based mechanism is also only as secure as the method used to configure the DNS server addresses on the host, so a host that cannot trust DHCPv6 cannot trust a DNS server learned through DHCPv6 either, unless it can authenticate all DNS responses, for example with DNSSEC.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker who can forge DNS or router messages could steer a host into the wrong prefix. The DHCPv6 and router advertisement methods need authentication to be safe against that.

viz.caption: THE FIVE ISSUES THE RFC MEASURES SOLUTIONS AGAINST

items.title: Issue #1: Detect synthesis
items.text: Is this IPv6 address translated? That tells the host a NAT64 is present.

items.title: Issue #2: Learn the prefix
items.text: The host needs the NSP or WKP to build an IPv6 address from an IPv4 address.

items.title: Issue #3: No DNS
items.text: The host has to learn the prefix without using DNS.

items.title: Issue #4: Changing prefix
items.text: A learned prefix goes stale when the host moves or the network changes it.

items.title: Issue #5: Several prefixes
items.text: A network may use more than one prefix, for example to spread load.
